lesson.title: Three Days in Pennsylvania: Gettysburg and the Turn of the War
lesson.summary: The three-day battle fought at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania from July 1 to July 3, 1863 repelled Robert E. Lee's second invasion of the North and, together with the fall of Vicksburg the same week, marked the turning point of the Civil War.
lesson.body:
Ten months after his retreat from Antietam, Robert E. Lee tried a Northern invasion a second time, hoping a major victory on Union soil might finally break Northern morale, strengthen the Confederacy's dwindling hopes for European recognition, and relieve war-torn Virginia by shifting the fighting, and the burden of feeding two armies, onto Pennsylvania farmland instead. The Army of Northern Virginia crossed into Pennsylvania in June 1863, and the Union Army of the Potomac, under a new commander, George Meade, who had taken charge only three days before the fighting began, moved to intercept it. The two armies collided almost by accident at the crossroads town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, on July 1, 1863, when Confederate troops searching for supplies ran into Union cavalry.

The fighting that followed over the next two days grew into the largest battle ever fought in North America, with roughly 165,000 soldiers engaged in total. On July 1, Confederate forces pushed Union troops back through the town to defensive high ground south of it, positions that would prove critical for the rest of the battle. On July 2, brutal fighting broke out at places that became etched into American memory, Little Round Top, the Wheatfield, the Peach Orchard, and Devil's Den, as Confederate attacks tried and failed to break the Union flanks. Union forces, aided by the timely defense of Little Round Top by troops including the 20th Maine, held their line along the high ground known as Cemetery Ridge.

On July 3, 1863, Lee gambled on a massive frontal assault against the center of the Union line, sending roughly 12,500 soldiers, most from Major General George Pickett's division, across nearly a mile of open ground in an attack remembered as Pickett's Charge. Union artillery and rifle fire tore the advancing lines apart, and the attack collapsed with devastating Confederate losses, effectively ending the battle. Lee, who reportedly took personal responsibility for the failure, withdrew his battered army back toward Virginia the next day. Total casualties over the three days reached an estimated 50,000, killed, wounded, captured, and missing, on both sides combined.

Gettysburg's significance was magnified by its timing: on July 4, 1863, the very day after Pickett's Charge failed, Confederate forces at Vicksburg, Mississippi surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant, giving the Union control of the entire Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy exactly as Winfield Scott's old Anaconda Plan had envisioned. Together, the two victories marked the war's clearest turning point, ending any realistic Confederate hope of winning through a decisive strike on Northern soil. Four and a half months later, on November 19, 1863, Lincoln traveled to Gettysburg to dedicate a national cemetery for the fallen and delivered the Gettysburg Address, a brief speech that redefined the war as a struggle to ensure that government of the people, by the people, and for the people would not perish from the earth.
